item.title: Seen on the Scene: Mix Sound for Film & TV 2026, Part 1
item.dc:creator: Clive Young
item.category: mix sound for film and TV
item.description: The annual Mix Sound for Film & TV event returned to Sony Pictures Studios on Saturday, September 26, packing the house with audio pros, amazing gear and more.
item.content:encoded:
Culver City, CA (September 30, 2026)—The annual Mix Sound for Film & Television event returned to the post-production facilities of Sony Pictures Studios on Saturday, September 26, and packed the house! More than 500 audio professionals came out to take in a full day of expert post-production sound panels, technology demos and sound profiles featuring some of the year’s biggest films!

With so much going on at the event, no single look back can adequately convey just how big it was and how many great panels, networking opportunities, product demos and more were available to check out, so we’re going to break it down, starting with Part 1 – The Mix Panels.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Mix may stage the event, but it also hosts some of the most eye-opening panels throughout the day, bringing top-name audio and music pros to the stage to share their hard-won insights and experiences with attendees. Each panel had something for everyone, from seasoned veterans to emerging professionals.

 

 

 

 

 

 

Come back tomorrow to see more of the day’s big events!

item.title: Oasis Sues Former FOH Engineer Over Tapes
item.dc:creator: Clive Young
item.description: Oasis has filed a lawsuit to prevent the sale of concert, soundcheck and rehearsal recordings captured by engineer Huw Richards.
item.content:encoded:
London, United Kingdom (September 30, 2026)—Stadium rockers Oasis had a hit with the song “Don’t Look Back In Anger,” but they might not be taking their own advice this week. The band filed an injunction Tuesday to prevent its former FOH engineer, Huw Richards, from auctioning off his archive of vintage Oasis board tapes, rehearsals and soundchecks.

The massive tape library was originally due to be sold on October 3 by Worcestershire, UK-based Littleton Auctions as part of an “Icons and Artifacts” music memorabilia auction, but has been withdrawn from sale, pending the outcome of the legal proceedings.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Putting the “sonic” in “Supersonic” for the band’s live shows, Richards mixed Oasis from 1995 through 2001, accumulating a staggering number of recordings in the process that traced the band’s commercial peak. The archive includes 63 concerts and more than 100 hours of rehearsals, soundchecks and band discussions, all captured direct from the house desk. The stash is spread across 209 DAT tapes, 73 cassettes and three MiniDiscs. Littleton Auctions listed the collection with an auction estimate upward of £1.6m (roughly $2.125m US).

The injunction was filed in a London court on Tuesday, listing Oasis Partnership, Sony Music and the group’s label, Big Brother Recordings, among its five claimants; defendants listed include the auction house, the engineer and Richards’ son Owain, who arranged the sale of his father’s items. When the auction was first announced, the younger Richards told multiple press outlets that he had previously attempted to sell the archive to the band, but that discussions had broken down, leading to the sale.

• Eminem Track Leak Case May Get Guilty Plea

As it stands, if the archive were to be sold, the new owner would only own the physical media itself, as the group would retain IP rights to the recordings’ contents, making any legal public release of the material without the band’s consent virtually impossible.

In the meantime, the rest of the Icons and Artifacts auction will go on as planned—and it will still include a number of Oasis items sourced from Huw Richards, including a guitar, amp, clothing, tour laminates, setlists, tour itineraries, crew gifts, a platinum record award and more.

item.title: Black Lava Studios Creates Immersive Mix Space at Home
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: To build a new immersive mix studio in a residential garage, Black Lava Studios turned to ASG.
item.content:encoded:
Emeryville, CA (September 30, 2026)—Steve Schatz is a veteran of post-production, having spent roughly a quarter-century working on film dubbing stages at Universal, Warner Bros., Sony, Disney and Skywalker Sound. When he decided to create his own immersive audio facility in his converted residential garage, Black Lava Studios was born.

Located in Sacramento, Black Lava Studios supports Dolby Atmos music mixing and mastering, film and documentary work, sound design, recording and quality control. To create a workspace based around his workflow, Schatz brought in Advanced Systems Group (ASG), which designed and supplied the studio’s 9.1.6 monitoring environment and advised on speaker placement, room correction, conversion and signal routing.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

For much of the process, Schatz coordinated with Collyer Spreen, Professional Technical Sales Engineer at ASG. “Collyer guided me through many of the intangibles of building a studio; the things you may not think about until you have lived with a room,” said Schatz. “They were incredibly patient. They loaned me equipment and gave me time to listen, work, and develop a real sense of what I wanted.”

To Spreen, however, it was a straightforward way to ensure Schatz was set up with the most appropriate environment to meet his production needs. Spreen explained, “Steve has spent his career in some of the best audio environments in the industry, so he knew exactly what a professional room should feel like. Our job was to help him translate that experience into a studio, work through the options with him, and make sure every part of the monitoring system supported the way he wanted to work.”

As a result, Black Lava Studios now sports 15 Neumann KH 150 loudspeakers, a KH 870 subwoofer and a Trinnov D-MON processor for monitoring control and room optimization. A Digital Audio Denmark AX64 interface accommodates analog, AES, Dante and MADI connections, allowing Schatz to move between sources and workflows without repeatedly reconfiguring the room. A Lynx Studio Hilo converter supports stereo and headphone monitoring.

• Oasis Sues Former FOH Engineer Over Tapes

The result is a consistent listening environment where Schatz can confidently assess creative choices across different types of projects. An early test came when he mixed a 13-minute documentary directed and edited by Thom Zimny for Bruce Springsteen’s Nebraska box set release last year.

“It was a chance to battle-test the room, and it came out beautifully,” said Schatz. “That was an important moment because it showed that the decisions we had made were working, not only technically, but creatively.”

item.title: 64 Audio Founder/CEO Belonozhko Steps Down
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Stewart Millager, previously 64 Audio’s COO, has been promoted to Fractional CEO.
item.content:encoded:
Vancouver, WA (September 30, 2026)—Vitaliy Belonozhko, founder and CEO of IEM manufacturer 64 Audio, is stepping away from his role leading the business on a day-to-day basis but will remain involved with the company.

Noting that he will remain involved “in the high-level, strategic decisions and initiatives,” Belonozhko said, “My decision stems from a personal need to step away from the full-CEO role and devote my primary focus to family needs. The intent behind this decision is to place an individual into this seat who has the capacity to drive the company towards reaching the goals and initiatives we have set, while accomplishing the company mission, vision, and values.”

• Oasis Sues Former FOH Engineer Over Tapes

In his place, previous COO Stewart Millager has been promoted to Fractional CEO. Nick Matev, previously CMO, has been named Chief Business Development Officer, and Filipp Sklyarov, previously Marketing Manager, has been promoted to Director of Sales & Marketing.

Belonozhko noted, “I am confident that Stewart will be able to successfully take on this new scope, due to his strong executive experience and leadership track record during his career.”

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Belonozhko founded the company in 2010 as 1964 Ears LLC., and grew it into one of the best-known in-ear monitor manufacturers in the pro-audio business. Taking the reins, Millager stated, “In this expanded role, my focus will remain on our people, our customers, and building the systems and culture that allow us to serve both exceptionally well. I’m honored to help lead 64 Audio into its next chapter while staying true to the values and commitment to quality that have brought us this far.”

item.title: Mix Tech Spotlight: Fairlight Live
item.dc:creator: Steve Harvey
item.description: Blackmagic Design debuts feature-rich platform for any and all types of live sound/broadcast production—and it’s free.
item.content:encoded:
New York, NY (September 30, 2026)—In July, Blackmagic Design announced the final release of its new software-based live audio mixer, Fairlight Live, following a public beta release earlier this year. Running on macOS or Windows machines, Fairlight Live is being marketed by Blackmagic Design as suitable for everything from simple audio and video podcasts to complex live sports broadcasts, offering a host of features essential to those applications, such as IFB and mix-minus feeds, extensive comms and test tone functionality, and AFV capabilities for over 100 cameras.

Indeed, the software is so feature-rich that it’s impossible to get into the granular details here. Taking a high-level view, Fairlight Live handles thousands of audio channels, dozens and dozens of main output, aux, matrix, mix-minus and subgroup buses, and VCA groups. Native Fairlight channel processing may be augmented by third-party AU and VST plug-ins. The software is compatible with Core Audio, ASIO devices and SMPTE 2110 broadcast workflows and supports surround and immersive audio mixing. Live sound production-focused features include snapshots, virtual soundcheck recording and a dedicated player for audio and MIDI cues.

Fairlight Live is available free of charge from Blackmagic Design’s website.

PLAYS WELL WITH EVERYONE

Anyone familiar with Fairlight’s history may recall that the company, founded in Australia, introduced one of the first DAWs with integrated sampling, in 1979. Initially popular with well-to-do musicians and producers (the system was not cheap), Fairlight’s products evolved as the company’s fortunes changed over the decades, coming to focus on audio post production applications starting in the 1990s. The one constant was that Fairlight systems shipped as a package with proprietary hardware, but after Blackmagic Design acquired Fairlight in 2016, the software was untethered from the dedicated editing/mixing hardware and integrated into the company’s DaVinci Resolve video postproduction software suite.

Fast-forward to 2026 and the software has been retargeted into a new package designed from the ground up for the full range of live productions, including performances and broadcast. The system can simply run on a Mac or Windows laptop, but for those who prefer a tactile mixing surface, the company has also introduced three Fairlight Live Audio Panel models with up to 40 faders. Fairlight Live supports AFV setups with up to 128 cameras when interfaced with many of Blackmagic Design’s ATEM multi-camera live production switchers.

Since the software supports USB, Thunderbolt and Ethernet and computer audio standards, it is relatively easy to integrate with many of today’s popular digital audio interfaces and mixing consoles. For example, if computer audio is already integrated into a church live sound or broadcast setup, then Fairlight Live will almost certainly work with it. In fact, a lot of the initial enthusiasm following the software’s release has come from the church sound market, as evidenced by YouTube videos demonstrating how users have implemented Fairlight Live with their existing setups. Further, support for OSC and Mackie MCU extends control to auxiliary devices so that, say, musicians can mix their own monitors, or production staff can operate comms with a tablet or other device.

The system can be run in several modes. In primary mode, the system is standalone, with the operator in full control. Remote mode may be enabled to allow another operator to control the crowd mics, monitors, talkback or other aspects of the show. On Air mode locks out remote operators to prevent accidental changes to the main outputs. Failsafe mode adds failover redundancy for, say, critical broadcast applications, with a secondary system mirroring the primary.

FEATURE-RICH

In operation, Fairlight Live offers the features and capabilities you would expect of high-end live production software. As with any such system, regardless of operational mode, there is some preproduction programming necessary to configure a mix (best handled through the Index, Fairlight Live’s function list view), capture snapshots (with channel and function iso masking), set preferences and so on. Everything can be changed or modified on the fly, of course. The GUI can be customized to show only the components of the mix the operator needs to see, including on a second screen. For broadcast applications, in addition to the expected input and output metering, Fairlight Live offers a menu of the 10 most common loudness metering standards, which may be displayed graphically and numerically.

A mix is set up in what Fairlight Live calls a Show, which not only saves the system-wide settings but also all associated audio files. Blackmagic Design has tested the system with more than 2,000 channels, and users online have demonstrated capturing 200 tracks or more into the onboard player/recorder for virtual soundchecks, so capacity is unlikely to be a barrier for most users.

Native processing includes six-band EQ, expander/gate, compressor and limiter. Channel strips are laid out on the left side of the mixer with buses on the right but can be freely rearranged.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Using Fairlight Live’s Chain FX plug-in (previously introduced in DaVinci Resolve), which supports six plug-ins, up to a total of 24 plug-ins may be inserted per channel or bus via the available four slots. Of course, there is ultimately a finite amount of compute available in any digital audio system, so adding large amounts of channel processing and third-party plug-ins could tax the system and add latency, depending on the number of buses also in use. Channels include delay compensation.

The mixer provides 2D, 3D and spherical pan controls supporting formats from mono and stereo to 5.1, plus up to 5th order Ambisonics (5OA) and Apple Spatial Audio Format (ASAF). A graphic visualization appears on the channel which, when selected, calls up controls related to the format, including rotation, spread and divergence, plus dedicated LFE routing and level where applicable.

LIVE AUDIO PANELS

The optional Fairlight Live Audio Panels feature 10, 20 or 40 motorized faders ($2,415, $3,845 and $8,245, respectively) with a large touch display per 10-channel bay. Channels may be freely assigned to any of 12 layers, potentially putting up to 480 channels under fader control. Fader flip swaps aux level control to the faders.

A combination of function, channel select and soft controls in a logical layout around each screen allow the user to manipulate whatever function is selected on the display. Buttons on the upper right control a player/recorder offering virtual soundcheck functions and iso recording of all inputs, a cue player—a sort of virtual cart machine—and snapshots. Control room monitoring, bus and group master, and talkback switching are accessed below those.

The rear panel includes a headphone jack (with a separate feed on the front), mic and talkback headset XLRs, XLR speaker outs, USB, and ST 2110 A/V network and control connections plus an HDMI connector. The 10-fader model supports battery-powered operation; the 20- and 40-fader versions have redundant power supplies.

For those working in A/V services or fixed installations, Fairlight Live, especially when integrated and synched with other pieces, can potentially centralize control of a multimedia show, from audio, MIDI and video to even lighting, or it could simply extend a church sound rig to manage a broadcast mix. The optional panels feature a rugged steel chassis, but it remains to be seen how well they stand up to the rigors of the road. Finally, for those whose interest is piqued by Fairlight Live but are seeking a more traditional DAW, DaVinci Resolve includes Fairlight’s dedicated sound design, recording, editing, sweetening and mixing software—and is also a free download from Blackmagic Design.

item.title: View from the Top: Yasmine Riechers, CEO, Georg Neumann GmbH
item.dc:creator: Tom Kenny
item.description: Yasmine Riechers, CEO of Neumann, discusses how the high-end pro audio brand is maintaining authenticity while still evolving for the future.
item.content:encoded:
New York, NY (September 29, 2026)—Over the past decade, under the leadership of Daniel and Andreas Sennheiser, the Sennheiser/Neumann company has been as active, dynamic and forward-thinking as any group in pro audio—entering new product categories, introducing a raft of new products, developing a complete end-to-end production workflow—while at the same time embracing its nearly century-old legacy of quality and innovation.

Yasmine Riechers joined Sennheiser Group in 2015, coming aboard to help develop Sennheiser Greater China, first as Director of Operations and later as Country Manager. In the early 2020s, she returned to Germany to head the Sennheiser Group’s Corporate Development Office. In March 2024, Riechers was named CEO of Georg Neumann GmbH.

Mix sat down with Riechers in January at the NAMM Show, then continued the discussion in the months that followed to explore her thoughts on legacy, adaptability and the excitement of what’s coming next.

Mix: You have an extensive background in technology and business; how and when did you get your start in pro audio?

Riechers: My academic background is in international business, but I was always drawn to the intersection of business and technology. Early in my career, I deliberately complemented my studies with hands-on experience through internships that exposed me to industrial environments and global operations.

My entry into the product business happened quite organically. A defining moment came when I was given the opportunity to help establish a production facility in China. What began as close involvement during the project phase quickly expanded into full operational responsibility. That experience gave me a very practical understanding of manufacturing processes, scalability and global supply chains.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

I then joined Sennheiser in 2015, a step that was both professional and personal. Having grown up near Hanover, Sennheiser was always part of my environment, and my family has longstanding ties to the company. Bringing together that personal connection with my passion for technology, products and brand-building felt like a natural choice—and it continues to shape how I lead today.

How did your years in China help to shape (or expand) your approach in developing a global business strategy?

My time in China was one of the most formative phases of my career. It gave me firsthand exposure to one of the world’s most dynamic and fast-moving markets and fundamentally shaped how I think about global business, innovation and scale.

Working in that environment taught me the importance of speed, adaptability and local relevance. In Europe, we often approach strategy with long planning cycles, whereas in China, market dynamics can shift within months. That experience helped me develop a much more agile and entrepreneurial mindset.

I was deeply involved in expansion projects, production development and cross-functional collaboration between global and local teams. One key learning was that successful global strategies cannot simply be exported from headquarters—they must be adapted to regional customer needs, cultural expectations and market realities.

China also showed me the value of integrated ecosystems. Technology, manufacturing, digital platforms and customer engagement are far more interconnected there, and that strongly influences how I think about future-ready business models today.

These experiences continue to shape my leadership approach at Neumann. Whether we are developing new product ecosystems, entering growth markets or strengthening global brand positioning, I try to balance long-term strategy with the flexibility to move quickly and stay close to the customer.

Now that Sennheiser USA has relocated to Nashville, are there plans to expand or otherwise modify Neumann’s U.S. presence?

This is not simply a relocation of offices—it is a deliberate step toward being closer to the creative heart of the professional audio industry in the U.S. Nashville is a global hub for artists, producers, engineers and studios, and proximity to that community truly matters.

When I visited in 2024, I was struck by the energy, connectivity and creative spirit of the city. It immediately felt like the right home for us. Being present where music and content are created every day allows us to listen more closely, deepen relationships and better understand evolving workflows. Our ambition goes beyond showcasing individual products; it is about being part of the creative community. You will see us placing greater emphasis on education, partnerships and direct engagement with creators and engineers.

How do you take a long-running, worldwide, gold-standard of a brand, one that is often associated with a single product category, into a world now dominated by software and AI?

This is one of the most important strategic questions for any legacy brand today, and I actually see it as a unique opportunity. The strength of Neumann lies in the trust and credibility we have built over nearly a century. We were there at the very beginning of professional audio, developing the first commercially available condenser microphone.

But even then, Neumann was never only about microphones. Georg Neumann’s vision was broader: He wanted to make sound last. At the time, that required microphones, cutting lathes, amplifiers and mixing desks. Today, the tools have evolved, but the mission remains exactly the same.

Modern creative workflows are no longer defined by isolated hardware. They are connected ecosystems that bring together hardware, software, immersive audio and, increasingly, AI-supported workflows. Our strategy is not about leaving our heritage behind, but about translating our legacy of precision, innovation and trust into the technologies shaping today’s creative world.

The challenge for any heritage brand is to evolve without losing authenticity. Our approach is to innovate from a position of authenticity— carrying forward what Neumann stands for and applying it to the future of audio production.

Can you expand on the idea of a full production ecosystem?

Enabling workflows has always been central to Neumann, because making sound last is ultimately what the brand stands for. In the past, professional recording was defined by large studios and fixed installations. Today, creativity is far more fluid. An artist might begin an immersive mix in a studio with a full 7.1.4 KH monitoring setup, then continue working on the same project from a hotel room using an MT 48 interface, NDH headphones and our RIME software.

Technology should adapt to creators—not the other way around—and enabling that flexibility is core to our strategy.

This is also why we explore new platforms and workflows. Our audio spatial positioning app, Virtual Immersive Studio (VIS), developed for Apple Vision Pro, is a great example. I often describe it as our “concept car” for the industry, because it demonstrates what immersive workflows could look like when technology becomes intuitive and almost disappears into the creative process.

At the same time, we remain deeply rooted in craftsmanship. Shortly after launching the Vision Pro app, we reissued the legendary M 50 microphone from the 1950s. That balance— heritage and innovation—defines Neumann.

Where do you see the best opportunities to grow the Neumann portfolio over the next 5 to 10 years?

The next decade is about evolving Neumann from a product brand into a true workflow standard. Our biggest opportunities lie in connected workflows—particularly in areas such as AoIP, immersive audio, software integration and emerging creator segments. The industry is clearly moving away from standalone products toward integrated ecosystems, and this aligns naturally with our strategy.

Geographically, we continue to see strong growth potential in Asia, while further expanding our presence in key creative hubs such as the U.K. and the U.S. At the same time, the next generation of creators works fluidly across professional studios, home environments and mobile setups. This is driving demand for tools that combine uncompromising audio quality with simplicity, flexibility and portability.

Our goal is not just to be relevant in five or ten years, but to build a brand that endures for the next hundred.

Your two-and-a-half-year anniversary as CEO is coming up. What have you learned? What would you consider some of the early successes?

The past two years have been incredibly exciting— and also very humbling. What I have learned most is how powerful the combination of strong heritage and a genuine willingness to evolve can be.

One early success I am particularly proud of is the clarity we have achieved around our end-toend strategy. We have moved beyond thinking in individual products and strengthened Neumann as a workflow brand—while remaining deeply connected to our craftsmanship and engineering roots.

item.title: Capitol Studios L.A. Updates with PMC
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Last Friday saw PMC Speakers take over Capitol Studios in Los Angeles for an event to mark the company’s 35th anniversary.
item.content:encoded:
Hollywood, CA (September 29, 2026)—Last Friday saw PMC Speakers take over Capitol Studios in Los Angeles for an event to mark the company’s 35th anniversary. The facility, located at the base of the famed Capitol Records Tower, has undergone a sizable renovation in recent years—an effort that included the installation more than 50 PMC  Speakers throughout the Tower and the half-dozen studios at its base.

The event included live performances from Melody Gardot, Grammy-nominated vocalist and pianist Sheléa and percussionist Kevin Ricard, and was attended by engineeres, producers, UMG executives and more.

“I can’t think of a more fitting venue in which to celebrate our 35 years,” said Peter Thomas, co-founder and chairman of PMC. “It is surely the most recognizable studio building in the world and now, having been fitted out with our new monitors, where better to share this anniversary with our customers, friends and the biggest names from the music industry.”

On the ground floor of the tower, Studio A, the largest of the spaces, with room for a 50-strong orchestra, has been fitted out with the new PMC10-4 main monitors and custom subwoofers. Nearfield monitoring in Studio A is provided by the PMC6 compact monitors. An identical installation can be found in Studio B.

For stereo and immersive audio mixing, Studio C is equipped with the PMC15 XBD for the left and right channels and PMC15 for the center. The PMC15 XBD builds on the legacy of the original BB5 XBD – the speakers that launched PMC into the world of professional audio and music making back in 1991. A mixture of Ci140s and Ci65s make up the surrounds and height channels, and two BST subwoofers supply the lower frequency information.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Two further stereo production/recording and mixing studios, D and E, have both been supplied with the PMC8-2 XBD system, with two additional PMC8-2 SUB subwoofers employed. Moving up to the first floor, Studio F, a Dolby Atmos mixing and QC suite, has twotwo.8 monitors for the left, center and right channels and Wafer1s for surround and height use.

Also located throughout the Capitol Studios facility, in various offices and boardrooms, are a selection of the PMC hi-fi speakers for playback, including prophecy models, and numerous Ci on-wall speakers.

item.title: Miking Jazz at Lincoln Center Performances for Sonic Honesty
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Todd Whitelock, a 13-time Grammy-winning engineer, discusses his miking choices at New York’s famed Jazz at Lincoln Center.
item.content:encoded:
New York, NY (September 29, 2026)—Key to the Amplified Art and Sound audio recording and mixing team’s day-to-day work at Jazz at Lincoln Center is its selection of tools.

Amplified Art and Sound LLC has been at the center of the institution’s archival recording, studio recording, broadcast, and streaming operations since 2021. Owner and chief engineer Todd Whitelock, a 13-time Grammy-winning engineer with a background at Power Station, Sony Classical Productions and Sony Music Studios, has long collaborated with the center’s founder and managing and artistic director Wynton Marsalis.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

“The greatest performers in the world play on our stages and as such, we take our responsibility to livestream and capture those performances very seriously,” Whitelock explains. “When our team first started with JALC, the goal was to bring a more ambient approach to recording that I’d done with Sony Classical so that we could purposefully capture these performances in a way that elevated them sonically while still being true to the players and their sounds they get on stage. Close miking alone doesn’t adequately capture the power of the orchestra in full swing.” He says that Marsalis had always envisioned that sound for the livestreams and records released by JALC’s label Blue Engine Records.

Whitelock often opts to use Schoeps mics, a choice influenced by his time at Sony Classical, where tonmeisters ​favored them for their pickup and minimal stage profile, an essential element required for orchestral recording. They have since become workhorse microphones for him both in the studio and live at JALC.

• Capitol Studios L.A. Updates with PMC

“Schoeps were the very first thing I asked for to hang as our main array,” he says. “We use seven Colette Series with MK 2 capsules hanging from the stage catwalks for all of our live performance recording sessions both in Rose Theater and The Appel Room.”

He comments, “The mark of a great microphone is their sonic honesty, in my opinion. The ability to capture the true characteristics of an instrument is always a challenge, and you want the microphone to do that without imparting too much unnecessary coloration on the results. I equate that to a photographer choosing the right lens for a closeup versus a landscape.”

item.title: In This System, the T is for Theater
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Der Josefstadt, located in Vienna, has installed a mixing system that enables engineers to mix performances from multiple venues.
item.content:encoded:
Vienna, Austria (September 29, 2026)—The sound department of the Theater in der Josefstadt, located in Vienna, has installed an SSL System T digital mixing system that enables engineers to mix performances from multiple venues.

Known locally as Die Josefstadt, the theater first opened in 1788, was rebuilt in 1822 and remains a notable cultural institution, staging both plays and musical productions. Together with its nearby sister venue, the smaller Kammerspiele, it now forms part of a shared production environment built around SSL’s System T platform.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

The Kammerspiele was the first of the two theaters to install an SSL System T in 2024. Raimund Hornich, the head of the sound department for both theatres, moved on to the upgrade for Die Josefstadt after the Kammerspiele installation. “I started in the job three years ago and at that time, both places had very old school mixing consoles,” he says. “I had to install a new system with a modern workflow for theatre productions nowadays and SSL provided that.”

• Capitol Studios L.A. Updates with PMC

​During the summer 2025 closed season, installation work began at Die Josefstadt on a similar system utilizing two 32-fader S500 surfaces. The effort was part of a major refit of the theater, which also included an AoIP network, a wideband Sennheiser multichannel wireless microphone system and a d&b audiotechnik PA system.

System T utilizes Open Sound Control (OSC) to provide real time control of audio objects using the System T user interface for a range of external renderers, directly from the System T user interface. “One of the features I value most is the integration with object-based workflows,” comments Hornich. This feature will allow Die Josefstadt’s operators to integrate Soundscape in the future while working within a System T ecosystem.

item.title: Low End Candy Fires Off Slingshot Plug-In
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Low End Candy has launched Slingshot, a reverse delay plug-in that allows DAW users to create and manipulate echoes.
item.content:encoded:
Carlsbad, CA (September 29, 2026)—Low End Candy has launched Slingshot, a reverse delay plug-in that allows DAW users to create and manipulate echoes that arrive before a sound instead of after.

While the typical method of printing a delay tail, reversing the audio, dragging it back in front of a note and then nudging it into place is straight-forward, any time a change is made to the tempo, note or arrangement, the reverse delay has to be remade. Slingshot approaches the problem by building that delay as an ordinary effect.

• Capitol Studios L.A. Updates with PMC

Users can apply the reverse delays using a number of different modes, starting with the default Aligned mode, which reports the lead-in to the DAW as latency, so the echo train lands exactly ahead of the transient and stops wherever the sound starts. Meanwhile, Live mode provides zero-latency monitoring while tracking; the resultant reversed echoes stack up and rush into the drop, built live from the user’s own audio.

Alternately, there’s Capture where users can play the sound once and Slingshot will print the lead-in as a WAV file trimmed to the transient and padded to a whole bar, ready to drag to the grid.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Other options include Feedback, affecting the number of repeats; Time, which can be set as free or tempo-synced; an ability to drag the echo train sideways to change its length, up or down to reshape the crescendo; and a choice of six (Clean, Tape, Analog, Diffuse, Ping-Pong, and Filtered) delay characters, with each repeat running back through the character.

33 factory presets are available across various categories to help Slingshot users get started.

Version 1.9.0 of Slingshot is now available for $49.00 USD.

item.title: DiGiCo Launches Quantum638 Mixing Console
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Staking out the middle ground between the Quantum852 and Quantum338 Pulse, DiGiCo’s Quantum638 is largely aimed at theatrical productions.
item.content:encoded:
New York, NY (September 28, 2026)—DiGiCo is launching its latest mixing console—the Quantum638, staking out the middle ground between the line’s Quantum852 and popular Quantum338 Pulse desks. The new offering is said to bring together elements from DiGiCo’s SD5 and SD7 consoles and hones them specifically to the needs of theatre sound teams. The Quantum638 is additionally available with an optional Quantum638T version designed specifically for theatrical productions.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Roughly the size of an SD7, the Quantum638 is available in single-engine and dual-engine versions, both with dual DMI card slots and hot-swappable PSUs, for a choice of preferred redundancy options. Outfitted with 256 input channels and 128 aux/sub-group busses, the new desk features three 17-inch (42cm) LCD high-resolution touchscreens; three 6.8-inch (17.3cm) TFT screens located adjacent to the fader bays; 38 100mm touch-sensitive motorized faders split into three worksurface sections with two dedicated Master faders; enhanced Macro buttons; dual headphone outputs; and more.

• Apple Music Hall Venue/Studio Complex to Open in London

When paired with DiGiCo’s optional “T” theatre software extension, the Quantum638T version adds functions like Auto Update, Aliases, Players, advanced CG programming tools,and Matrix Nodal Delays for plays and musicals.

The new console additionally offers a 48×48 matrix with full processing, plus Quantum Range features such as 128 Nodal Processing instances, 64 insertable Mustard Processing strips, 16 Spice Rack slots and True Solo functionality. The desk sports onboard Dante and other connectivity options, including a built-in Fourier Interface Card for native worksurface compatibility with Fourier Audio’s transform.engine platform.

Lined up beneath the center screen are newly enhanced Macro buttons, and there are four designated channel Macros, meaning the Macro moves with the channel depending on the console layout.

The rear panel features 32-bit mic/line inputs, eight 32-bit line outputs, four AES/EBU inputs (eight channels), and four AES/EBU outputs (also eight channels), as well as a DSub37 GPI and DSub37 GPO (16 inputs and 16 outputs), one set of MIDI In/Thru/Out, and a set of XLR SMPTE LTC I/O. Additional connections include four switched Ethernet ports and eight sets of MADI I/O, giving up to eight MADI interfaces or up to four redundant MADI interfaces at 48 kHz or four interfaces at 96 kHz.

item.title: Mastering the Mix Stereovault – A Mix Real-World Review
item.dc:creator: Rob Tavaglione
item.description: Our crack review team put Mastering The Mix's Stereovault plug-in the test and declared "Ultrawide mixes? Not a problem anymore."
item.content:encoded:
MIX VERDICT: MASTERING THE MIX STEREOVAULT
THE TAKEAWAY: “A typical modern mix could have Stereovault all over it in a variety of ways, utilizing the full spectrum of powers.”
COMPANY: Mastering the Mix • www.masteringthemix.com
PRICE: $80
PROS:
• Deep tool kit.
• Creatively fun.
CONS:
• So much power could be easy to abuse.

New York, NY (September 28, 2026)—I was starting to get a little concerned, as everybody seems to like ultra-wide mixes these days—more than I do at least. My width-creating plug-ins do a fine job on individual tracks, but with full mixes, the bottom-end loses power, punch evaporates and image stability becomes unpredictable. I’ve had difficult dialogues with clients about width and needed a solution; it appears that Stereovault has solved my problem.

Stereovault is a stereo image processor that tackles the entire issue of widening and narrowing of just about any source, in one multi-faceted, multi-methodology, complete plug-in.

A half-dozen Tabs can be used individually or together, and they all operate with multiple frequency bands, up to six each, allowing a level of deep control previously unseen. For the most invisible processing (mixes or mastering), the global Transparent mode is recommended, utilizing the exact same frequency bands/divisions across all Tabs. Conversely, Flexible mode allows the assigning of different frequency bands on each Tab, creating opportunity for wilder, not as phase-stable, processing.

Auditioning Tabs is made comfortable with level matching, individual bypasses and graphics that do a good job of visualizing the madness you sonically create as you invariably push parameters to extremes. The artistry lies in their ability to interact with each other for surgically complex image manipulation. The six Tabs are:

Spread: MTM calls this the cleanest way to widen, using Mid/ Side processing. Diffuse mode uses Gerzon per-band diffusion transparently, Vintage uses frequency-splitting techniques ideal for altering mono sources.

Creative: As implied, this Tab allows for the most extreme and interesting uses, employing one of five processes: Stretch (using comb filtering), Space (a tight and diffuse reverb), Haas (short panned delays), Chorus (short modulated delays) and Flux (slowly creeping movement, for long sustained sources).

Panorama: Allows standard panning, not full-bandwidth, but individually for each frequency band; or the oddly named Skew, which is actually reversing/swapping the placement within each band.

Rotate: Allows processing by rotating the signal, with stereo control or Mid/Side independence.

Width: Uses mid and side level controls, Blend mode swaps the two, and Balance allows individual channel level control.

Clean: Uses Mid/Side EQ for tight, surgical processing with the least phase problems.

As with many MTM plug-ins, Smart mode will analyze a portion of your audio and recommend a variety of settings—source-dependent, genre-dependent and ranging from subtle to animated. Analysis asks you to first pick between Mix, Bass, Drums, Music and Vocals; then you must choose between limited choices of Country, Electronic, Hip Hop, Pop and Rock. Finally, the four choices for each genre include Focused, Balanced, Wide and Super Wide. You’re either done at this point, or able to further tweak the recommendation or try other choices (there’s also a bunch of not-analysis- based presets, too).

• Discover more pro audio reviews—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

If you’d rather emulate one of your favorite stereo images, you can always load a reference file (drag and drop) and have Stereovault do all the work under the hood. You can widen your skill set (no pun intended) by seeing what processes Stereovault cleverly chose, and then further manipulate them.

With such a large plate of options, some deep analysis, metering and visualization control is necessary. Thankfully, these controls are hidden as pop-ups, keeping the GUI cleaner. The Visualizer window permits extensive control of the visual display’s responsiveness, with speed, phase and amplitude options. I/O obviously controls routing, allowing mono, Mid/Side and reversing options. Trim controls input and output gain, in stereo or Mid/Side. Scope utilizes a Lissajou display for stereo correlation and phase.

IN SESSION

I mentioned that I’ve had width problems as of late, so right off the bat, I tackled a recent power ballad mix that I had gotten just barely sufficiently wide using mix skills, without widening plugs, at least not on the mix bus. I selected four frequency bands and clicked Analyze, as Stereovault inspected about 10 seconds of the mix’s loudest portion. I then selected Rock from the genre-based pull-down and listened to Stereovault’s suggestions. They were very good, but, as you’ve likely already guessed, an old-hand like myself would rather dig deeper and mine for gold.

With some very careful adjustments using Transparent mode, and Clean and Width Tabs, I dialed in the ideal. I made the bottom-end mono below 60 Hz, kept the low-mids untouched, ever so slightly widened the high-mids and gave some moderate width to the high end. The result? My subs hit with more solidity, my low-mids stayed warm and “out of the way,” my upper-mids saw no change in vocal level or dominance (just size), and the drums opened up with non-distracting width in the overheads only.

I later tackled some mastering work with Stereovault, work that needed heavier lifting and careful decision-making across 10 not-all-that-consistently- mixed songs. With Transparent mode, with mostly Width or Clean (and a little use of Spread for interest and Rotate to rebalance left-to-right), I got that LP in shape better than I could have without Stereovault, and did it a lot faster than I expected. It deserves mention that I neatly narrowed a couple of spots with Stereovault—not as glamorous, but uniquely powerful and equally important!

• Apple Music Hall Venue/Studio Complex to Open in London

That’s all fine and subtle, but sometimes (okay, often) it’s very satisfying to take a mono source, spread it out like crazy and push it to the periphery of a mix. Many plug-ins are capable of this process, and I have more than a few, but Stereovault made them all seem a bit limited. Spread is great fun, Panorama is downright twisted and Creative is a rabbit hole of epic proportion. I’m not being hyperbolic here. The ability to tug, stretch and treat audio like taffy is powerful, but to do all that with frequency-band specificity is out of this world! As if this weren’t enough, I haven’t even automated such madness yet. I think I’m going to be testing someone’s patience at the next attended mix session

And let’s not forget sound design(ers), who might actually use all of Stereovault’s tabs and modes the most profoundly. It’s not hard to imagine some automated Panorama or Creative stretch effect realistically following on-screen action, or conversely a multi-tab, Flexible-mode, automated Spread and Rotate mind-warp for some sci-fi bizarreness.

THE FINAL MIX

And there lies the ultimate strength of Stereovault: the overall versatility. Veterans can dig in well beyond the elbows if they wish, as the sheer number of controls, choices and techniques is limitless and everything functions properly. The only fear is bad taste. For those who don’t revel in difficulty, the analysis, recommendations and reference-matching are likely sufficient, with deep control of parameters not necessary.

A typical modern mix could have Stereovault all over it in a variety of ways, utilizing the full spectrum of powers: width to the drum kit, slow drift to pads, mono-compatible freq-specific size to bass, mono’ing the subs, animating the vocal and warping some elements until they tickle the ear dancing outside the bulk of the soundstage. Maybe even subtly across the whole mix. Ultrawide mixes? Not a problem anymore.

item.title: MCCC Students Head to Muscle Shoals
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: MCCC students recorded original music with veteran session pros at the first Muscle Shoals Recording Residency.
item.content:encoded:
Muscle Shoals, AL (September 28, 2026)—The town of Muscle Shoals, Alabama isn’t the largest in the state, but its musical legacy might be. It’s home to both FAME Recording Studios and Muscle Shoals Sound Studio, both of which have hosted countless top music acts as they’ve recorded often legendary tracks. It’s a legacy that many have heard of, but few have experienced first-hand—but now you can include 15 students from the Sound Recording and Music Technology program of Montgomery County Community College among them.

In mid-August, the MCCC students traveled from their campus in Blue Bell, Pennsylvania to the storied studios for the inaugural Muscle Shoals Recording Residency, an immersive experience that placed them inside the studios as they recorded two original songs written by their group. Helping bring the tracks to life were veteran Muscle Shoals musicians Spooner Oldham, Will McFarlane, Clayton Ivey and Justin Holder.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

SRT Director David Ivory, a Grammy-nominated producer and engineer, organized the Residency, arranging that students would work with studio professionals to record music and sound, set up equipment, develop arrangements and evaluate performances. Ivory said students learned that making a great record requires more than technical knowledge. “It requires listening, communication, musicianship, collaboration,” he said, “and creative decision-making.”

As part of the process, the students watched as the team of seasoned session pros encountered the students’ new songs for the first time and began building arrangements in real time. “The moment I will remember most is watching Spooner Oldham play the Wurlitzer for my good friend Shaun’s original song,” said student Zach Wheitsel. “I was so honored to be in the room for this, and to say that I am beyond happy for my friend to have had this experience would be selling my feelings short.”

The inaugural Muscle Shoals Recording Residency was designed as the beginning of an ongoing experiential-learning opportunity for MCCC students, and planning is already underway for the next Residency and working to expand experiential-learning opportunities for students in the SRT program.

• Apple Music Hall Venue/Studio Complex to Open in London

“This first Residency showed us what’s possible,” Ivory said. “Now we want to build on it and give another group of students this opportunity. This wasn’t just about learning how records were made in Muscle Shoals. It was about giving our students the chance to discover what they’re capable of making themselves.”

As it stands, MCCC’s Sound Recording and Music Technology program has a considerable resources for students at its Blue Bell and Pottstown, PA campuses, working with pro-level equipment. The Blue Bell campus sports a mixing suite, outfitted with a Solid State Logic SSL 9000K 56-input console, that can tackle immersive Dolby Atmos mixes with its Genelec-based 7.1.4 system.

item.title: Catching Sound Waves at Virginia Beach Super Girl Surf Festival
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: A massive dBTechnologies P.A. provided audio for 22 concerts during the Virginia Beach Super Girl Surf Festival.
item.content:encoded:
Virginia Beach, VA (September 28, 2026)—The numbers don’t lie; the first Virginia Beach Super Girl Surf Festival, held earlier this month over Labor Day Weekend, was a massive undertaking, with the on-the-beach event hosting 4,000 female athletes participating across 14 sports; 24 fitness and wellness classes; 22 concerts; and more. Providing much of the production for the event were Shadow Mountain Productions, Cardon Audio Productions and Media Minds.

The World Surf League competition drew fans from far and wide to its festival village, as well as to see the music lineup, which included Switchfoot, CeeLo Green, Lupe Fiasco, Gym Class Heroes, B.o.B, Collie Buddz, Bryce Vine and HIRIE, among others. The audience area was estimated at approximately 200 feet wide and 500 feet deep. An Allen & Heath dLive S7000 served as the front-of-house console, paired with a dLive S5000 at monitors, while an Avid S6L was brought in for Switchfoot’s headline set. dBTechnologies DVX DM15 wedges covered stage monitoring, supplemented by Shure Axient Digital PSM in-ear systems and ULX-D wireless.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Shadow Mountain Productions supplied the majority of the production package and provided lighting and video for the festival. Cardon Audio Productions contributed dBTechnologies VIO S118 subwoofers and VIO L1608 line array modules, while additional VIO L1610 modules and VIO S218 subwoofers were cross-rented from Baltimore-based Media Minds. Cam Cardon of Cardon Audio Productions designed and deployed the loudspeaker system and served as system technician, A1 and front-of-house engineer. Brandon McMeen mixed monitors, with several touring acts bringing their own engineers.

The main P.A. was built around left and right arrays of 10 VIO L1610 three-way line array modules. Two VIO S118 subwoofers were flown in line with each array, extending low-frequency support from the same elevation as the mains. Ten VIO S218 dual-18-inch subwoofers were deployed on the ground, with two cabinets positioned behind the forward line to create an end-fire array and control low-frequency energy behind the system. Four compact VIO L1608 modules provided front-fill coverage across the first rows.

• Apple Music Hall Venue/Studio Complex to Open in London

“The system sounded phenomenal,” said Cardon. “I was impressed by the amount of clarity we had hundreds of feet away. The throw from the L1610s was really impressive. The subwoofers sounded punchy and clean, and you could feel them all the way down the beach. The L1610 and L1608 sound very similar, so using the L1608 as front fill integrated seamlessly into the overall system.”

item.title: Griffith Observatory Theater Updates Audio System
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: The revamped audio system is inside the Griffith Observatory's Leonard Nimoy Event Horizon Theater.
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles, CA (September 28, 2026)—Perched above Los Angeles, the Griffith Observatory is as famous for its appearances in endless movies and TV shows as it is for educating millions of visitors over the years as to the mysteries of the skies. Much of that work in done in the facility’s Leonard Nimoy Event Horizon Theater, a 190-seat auditorium that recently underwent a sizable audio system update with the help of audiovisual technology specialist Solotech and consultant TheatreDNA.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

The theater is used daily to host programs, presentations and panels, but increasingly they were being interrupted by feedback from the existing house system. “We recognized the need for a solution that could address the unwanted reflections and uncontrolled audio challenges, without disrupting the theater’s strict aesthetic values,” said Patrick So, theater programs manager at Griffith Observatory. “We worked closely with Solotech and TheatreDNA, who guided us through a range of potential options while assessing coverage, clarity, and visual impact.”

In turn, the two companies settled on a recommendation of Renkus-Heinz ICONYX Gen 5 loudspeakers for the facility, with a single ICONYX IC16-RD model installed behind the projection screen upstage of where speakers stand to present. While the Leonard Nimoy Event Horizon Theater retained a dedicated playback system for film screenings, the IC16-RD was introduced exclusively for spoken word events.

“The beam steering capabilities allow for precise vertical coverage control, directing sound towards the audience while reducing energy on the reflective surfaces, ultimately helping to improve speech intelligibility and maintain consistent SPL from the front of the auditorium to the back,” Marc Nutter of Solotech explained.

• Apple Music Hall Venue/Studio Complex to Open in London

The wider AV system is built around a QSC network that brings audio, video, and control into a streamlined interface, allowing museum staff to prepare and operate daily programs and special events without requiring in-depth technical knowledge.

Since the debut of the new audio system, the audience experience inside the Leonard Nimoy Event Horizon Theater has improved noticeably. “The upgrade from the old system was immediately clear,” So reveals. “With the IC16-RD, there’s no more feedback when presenters speak into the microphones and the entire audience can hear even the most subtle details. The immense effort that everyone has put in has led to a far more immersive and engaging experience that fully lives up to the expectations of the Griffith Observatory.”

item.title: Mix Live Blog: Update That Firmware!!
item.dc:creator: Steve La Cerra
item.description: One of the rules of being on tour is never do a firmware update on the road. And then comes that one night when....
item.content:encoded:
Nottingham, UK (September 25, 2026)—One of the rules of being on tour is never do a firmware update on the road. Wait until you’re in the shop, with access to reliable internet and phone, when you have a reasonable expectation of getting tech support if needed (while maintaining your sanity). Truth.

And, so, sometimes firmware updates get overlooked because we’re too busy, um… working!

I’ll do it after this run of dates… I’ll do it when I’m sure the update is solid (that sounds like an iOS conundrum!).

I’m currently on tour in the UK and Europe running FOH for Jon Anderson & The Band Geeks tour, “Performing Yes Epics, Classics and More.” I’ve had the pleasure of working with the folks at 22live Ltd. (Redditch, UK), who are totally on point; our systems techs, Nick, Tom and Ryan, are making these shows an absolute pleasure.

We’re running Yamaha DM7s at FOH and monitors, and the other day, we encountered a mystery. As I have quoted Captain James T. Kirk in the past, “… I don’t like mysteries. They give me a bellyache, and I got a beauty right now.” Oh, yeah.

Our day at the Royal Concert Hall in Nottingham earlier this week went something like this…

3:00 P.M., Line Check

Our Yamaha DM7s are connected to two 32-channel RIO 3224 D2 RIOs with 50 inputs from the stage, and two playback channels for walk-in and walk-out music from FOH. Line check is fine. The band is rehearsing and I’m getting a feel for the room. This one is going to be diﬃcult. It’s a great space for a symphony orchestra, but for an amplified show with a rock band? Not so much.

4:00 P.M.-ish

My merch seller, Zak, has arrived and I have to leave my desk to check in with him. The previous venue made an absolute mess of our merch, and I’m sure the count was wrong, which makes today’s count more critical. Have I mentioned how much of a pain in the arse it can be to be a tour manager? Don’t do it!!! Unless you’re a glutton for punishment (like me).

Zak counts in all of approx. 700 pieces of merch (God bless him) and sends me the info. As suspected, the previous venue botched it. We log in the correct numbers. Meanwhile, the band is onstage working out some parts and getting their rigs dialed in before Jon arrives.

5:00 P.M., Security Meeting (I’m running late)

Jon is on stage doing his soundcheck and I’ve already missed the first song. Not good. Depending upon the day, he might only soundcheck two or three songs, but luckily for me, three songs can easily take 30 minutes. By the time I get to FOH, they’re almost done with the second song. I unmute my desk and the mix sounds weird, like the lead vocal mic has a different band member singing into it….

…because it does. One of the backing vocal mics is coming down Jon’s lead vocal channel. I ask my monitor engineer Drew Gantert if he’s having the same issue, and even from across the venue I can tell he’s looking at me like I should be wearing a straight jacket (which is debatable).

Knowing that I’m about as graceful on a touchscreen as Jackson Pollock was with a can of paint on canvas, I start checking settings in the DM7: Dante setup shows my two RIOs, connected and sync’d. Dante patch shows that, indeed, the two RIOs are connected to inputs 1 through 32 and 33 through 64, respectively. Channels 1 through 32 (the first stage box) are patched 1:1, showing up where they should. But starting at channel 33, everything is messed up. Input 33 (RIO #2, channel 1) is feeding channels 33 and 34. But not at the monitor desk. I haven’t been this disoriented since I accidentally ate a poison mushroom at Woodstock in 1969 (no, I didn’t, and no, I wasn’t).

• Mix Sound for Film & TV Complete Program Guide!

Nick (soon to be St. Nick, Father Christmas notwithstanding) and I try the usual remedies: We recheck the input patch (nothing wrong there), we recheck the Dante patch (nothing wrong there either).  We recall yesterday’s scene (which worked fine), and it exhibits the same symptoms. We recall a blank startup scene; same thing. We restart the desk and restart the RIO to no avail.

Meanwhile, Drew is not experiencing any of the same problems in monitor world. While I’m busy scratching my head, he searches the symptoms online and discovers that this is a known bug that was fixed in DM7 firmware V2.00: Dante patches between DM7 and mounted Dante devices may be unintentionally offset. Yup, that about sums it up. And a quick trip to the main menu on the DM7 verifies that we are (both) running firmware V1.75.

If you find yourself in a similar situation, you can check the firmware version by navigating to the Main menu (upper-right corner of the touchscreen), and selecting the General tab, at which point it will show the version of software currently installed.

Here’s the fix:

  • Dismount the RIO by pressing Setup. Navigate to I/O Device > Dante Setup. Tap the Device Mount Tab. Select the RIO you want to disconnect. Press Unmount.
  • Unpatch the inputs.
  • Reboot the console, then the RIO.
  • Remount the RIO
  • Repatch the inputs

This should cure the issue.

We proceed. It works. Yay! I’m doing my best not to flip out. What if this bug returns during the show? Yikes. Our fail-safe is to double-patch Jon’s main lead vocal microphone to a spare channel on the first RIO, so I’ll have it on channel 20 as well as channel 36.

7:30 P.M., Showtime

The show opens with “Close to the Edge,” and I make some adjustments now that the room is full. Strange, the room sounds much drier than it did during soundcheck. There’s a section of the song where I splash a long delay on Jon’s voice. I’m turning up the FX send, but I can’t hear any delay. And why are my background vocals so low in level?

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

Grrrrrr. I pull up my FX returns and none of them are showing any activity. They were all unpatched when we reset the RIOs. Awesome! Oddly, all of the sends remained patched. I’m repatching the returns while trying to mix the show, busier than a centipede at a toe-counting contest. What remains of my brain realizes that it’d be a good idea to pull down the DCA master for my FX before I hot-patch the FX outputs to the return channels.

I get through the patch and hold my breath while I slowly raise the FX master. Ahhhh, there it is… I splash another delay on Jon’s vocal, and this time, I hear the delay. All is well in the world—just in time for “Perpetual Change.”

item.title: Mixed In Key Wingman 3.0 Debuts
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: The music production plug-in returns with new features, including expanded chord editing, guitars performances and genre-specific drums.
item.content:encoded:
Miami, FL (September 25, 2026)—Mixed In Key has released Wingman 3.0, a free update to its music production plug-in that suggests chord progressions and basslines based on audio captured from a producer’s DAW.

The new 3.0 edition adds a variety of features, expanding on the plug-in’s chord-editing tools as well as adding vintage and modern guitar performances and offering a selection of genre-specific drums for users to work with.

Since Wingman suggests chord progressions based on the music currently in the producer’s DAW, Version 3.0 now provides more control over those suggestions, allowing users to rinsert passing chords between existing chords; replace individual chords and choose how frequently the harmony changes; resize, split, or remove chord regions; and audition each edit against the source audio—and it’s all done within the plug-in.

• Mix Sound for Film & TV Complete Program Guide!

Throughout, the original audio remains unchanged; the plug-in provides musical ideas to audition against it, then edit and export back into the session as desired. As a result, users can try different ideas—new chords around a vocal, find harmony for a sample, or try a different bassline for a remix—with a minimum of effort.

Version 3.0 also adds acoustic and electric guitar performances recorded by live musicians, thus retaining the performance’s articulation and variation. The recordings adapt to the selected chord progression, so producers can hear their chord ideas played as guitar parts rather than only through a synth or piano sound.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

A new Drums channel adds genre-based patterns for sections such as verses, hooks, and bridges, with separate kick and transition controls. Producers can audition patterns alongside their chord and bassline ideas and choose the elements they need. The full drum part or just individual elements can be exported for further work in the DAW.

Wingman 3.0 is available now for macOS and Windows as a one-time purchase with no subscription.

item.title: AutoTune Advanced Pitch Correction Plug-In Launches
item.dc:creator: Mix Staff
item.description: Debuting today, AutoTune Advanced is the new flagship edition of Antares’ long running pitch correction software.
item.content:encoded:
Santa Cruz, CA (September 25, 2026)—Debuting today, AutoTune Advanced is the new flagship edition of Antares’ long running pitch correction software. Based around a fresh start rebuild from the ground up, the software adds a new feature—a patent-pending “DVA engine” that recognizes vibrato singing—and an overall updated Auto-Mode pitch algorithm.

Antares reports that the updated Auto-Mode pitch algorithm represents the largest engineering investment in the AutoTune algorithm since its introduction; the DVA engine, which aims to provide vibrato detection and preserve it in order to retain character, is built on top of the updated algorithm.

• Mix Sound for Film & TV Complete Program Guide!

The DVA feature includes a real-time vibrato visualizer that shows what it hears, as it hears it. Conversely, if a performance could use some vibrato, the new creative Vibrato FX can add it, with sine, square, saw, or triangle waves controlled by rate and cut/boost controls.

Also new with AutoTune Advanced is a new Live mode that provides real-time monitoring, reporting plug-in latency of 0.84 ms at 44.1 kHz [buffer size, host]. Users have the option of working in Low Latency mode for responsive tracking, or High Quality mode for higher fidelity.

Elsewhere, the updated Formant Designer shapes vocal timbre, plus there’s now a custom scale workflow and a new 78-note Visual Keyboard. MIDI Perform turns a MIDI controller into a hands-on control surface for Advanced itself, allowing users to ride them in real time, or use them to write automation straight into a mix.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

The new plug-in also comes with a library of presets created by Grammy-winning producers and artists, including Julian Marley, Ann Mincieli, Tom Norris, Benjamin Thomas and others.

AutoTune Advanced is available as a perpetual license or as part of the AutoTune Unlimited subscription. A free trial to AutoTune Unlimited is available.

item.title: Sennheiser Spectera SKM Handheld Transmitter – A Mix Product of the Week
item.dc:creator: Steve La Cerra
item.description: Sennheiser is shipping its Spectera SKM handheld transmitter, completing the company’s core line of Spectera WMAS products.
item.content:encoded:
New York, NY (September 25, 2026)—Sennheiser is now shipping the Spectera SKM handheld transmitter, completing the company’s core line of Spectera products, which utilize WMAS (Wireless Multichannel Audio System) technology. The SKM offers ultra-low-latency (1.0 mS) wireless audio while providing the continuous monitoring and remote configuration features paramount to high-level productions.

The SKM employs an integrated control channel for continuous synchronization, status reporting and remote management. Bidirectional communication with the Spectera Base Station enables audio transmission, as well as real-time monitoring of battery status, RF performance, RSSI (Received Signal Strength Indicator), audio level, RF interference and link quality. The Spectera system also supports remote configuration of microphone gain and filtering, as well as over-the-air firmware updates.

• Mix Sound for Film & TV Complete Program Guide!

The SKM features robust metal construction, AES-256 encryption and an OLED display.

It utilizes the same BA 70 or BA 70 2.2 rechargeable batteries as the Spectera SEK bodypack. Battery run time is stated as up to seven hours; battery status can be viewed on the SKM’s display by pressing and holding the Control button found on the end cap.

The SKM is compatible with a wide range of microphone capsules, including the Sennheiser MMK 965-1, MMD 945-1 and MME 865-1, and the new Neumann KK 104 A and KK 105 A capsule heads.

• Discover more pro audio news—get a free Mix SmartBrief subscription!

The SKM is available in UHF (470–608 MHz and 630–698 MHz) and 1.4 GHz (1350–1400 MHz and 1435–1525 MHz) variants while taking full advantage of Sennheiser WMAS technology, whereby an engineer can add the SKM as another device within the Spectera wideband system in lieu of adding an individual receiver channel and coordinating an additional narrowband frequency as required by conventional narrowband wireless systems. WMAS simplifies RF planning while providing increased resistance to dropouts, as compared to narrowband wireless systems.

Specifications for the SKM include frequency response 20 Hz to 20 kHz; RF transmission power up to 50 mW (may be limited by local regulations); dimensions 196mm (7.72 inches) L x 40mm (1.57 inches).

The Sennheiser SKM is now available at a street price of around $2,000.
